chunks: From him, from al-‘Abbās, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Ḥarīz, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn Abī Ya‘fūr, from Abī ‘Abd Allāh عليه السلام, who said:

I said to him: A man sees in sleep and feels desire, then he wakes up and looks but finds nothing; then after a short while, it comes out. He said: “If he is ill, then let him perform ghusl (ritual bath), and if he is not ill, then there is nothing upon him.” He said: I said to him: So what is the difference between the two? He said: “Because when a man is healthy, the fluid comes with a strong gush, and if he is ill, it does not come except afterward.”

key_terms.الشَّهْوَةَ: sexual desire felt during the dream
key_terms.الْمَاءُ: the fluid referred to in the ruling
key_terms.بِدَفْعَةٍ قَوِيَّةٍ: with a strong gush, indicating the manner of discharge
key_terms.صَحِيحًا: healthy, in contrast to illness in this ruling
key_terms.مَرِيضًا: being ill, which affects the legal ruling here

ai.seo_question: Does delayed discharge after sleep require ghusl (ritual bath) in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling about ghusl (ritual bath) in a case where sexual desire is experienced during sleep but no discharge is found immediately upon waking. It distinguishes between a healthy person and an ill person, stating that delayed discharge in the case of illness requires ghusl, while otherwise there is no obligation.
